title: Plan 9
topic: Plan 9 from Bell Labs — the distributed operating system, viewed purely as technology: per-process namespaces, the 9P protocol, file servers, mount/bind/union directories, plumbing, and its security model

concepts.title: The Plan 9 Model
concepts.brief: Part 1 — the intro. The core ideas a reader needs before anything else: resources as file hierarchies, a single uniform protocol to reach them, and a private, per-process namespace that assembles those hierarchies into the view a program sees. Ground it in the 'Plan 9 from Bell Labs' overview paper (https://css.csail.mit.edu/6.824/2014/papers/plan9.pdf). No history, no author biography — just the design and why the three pillars compose.

concepts.title: Namespaces
concepts.brief: The per-process namespace as the central abstraction: what a namespace is, how it is built, how it is inherited and mutated, and what it buys you (customization, transparency, and the disappearance of most special-case system calls).

concepts.title: The 9P Protocol
concepts.brief: The wire protocol itself: fids, qids, the T-message/R-message pairs (version, auth, attach, walk, open, create, read, write, clunk, remove, stat, wstat), message framing, tags and concurrency, 9P2000 vs the earlier version, and the 9P2000.u/.L dialects. Be precise — this is the spine of the book.

concepts.title: File Servers
concepts.brief: Writing and using file servers: kernel devices (#c, #p, #s and friends) vs user-level servers, the lib9p/9pfile serving loop, srv(3)/the /srv registry, exportfs, synthetic file trees as interfaces, and what makes a good file-server interface design.

concepts.title: Mount, Bind, and Union Directories
concepts.brief: The namespace-construction operators: bind(2)/mount(2), the MREPL/MBEFORE/MAFTER/MCREATE flags, union directories and how lookup and create resolve through them, /bin as a union, unmount, and the namespace(6)/ns(1) description language.

concepts.title: Process Namespaces
concepts.brief: How namespaces and processes interact: rfork(2) and its RFNAMEG/RFCNAMEG/RFFDG/RFPROC/RFMEM/RFENVG flags, namespace inheritance and copy-on-fork semantics, /proc as the process interface, and per-process device slots such as /dev/cons.

concepts.title: Plumbing
concepts.brief: The plumber(4) as inter-application message routing: plumb messages and their attributes, the plumbing(6) rule language (matching, rewriting, ports), /mnt/plumb, and the canonical acme/plumb workflow — an interprocess bus built, of course, as a file server.

concepts.title: Security and the Capability Model
concepts.brief: Security as namespace design: no setuid, authentication factored out into factotum(4) and secstore, the auth(2)/AUTH messages in 9P, /dev/caphash and /dev/capuse capabilities for changing user id, the hostowner concept, and how a restricted namespace replaces most privilege.

notes: Requested brief: a very focused book on Plan 9 for a technically savvy reader. Sharp focus on the technology only — NOT the history, NOT the authors. Not verbose; get to the point. Part 1 is an introduction to Plan 9 grounded in the overview paper; Part 2 covers namespaces, the 9P protocol, file servers, mount/bind/union directories, process namespaces, plumbing, and the security/capability model. Explicitly OUT of scope, do not cover: the Plan 9 graphics stack, the C compiler/toolchain, Inferno, CPU architecture support, and historical Unix comparisons (brief technical contrast is fine where it clarifies a mechanism, but no historical narrative). Do web research for accuracy. Reference material: https://css.csail.mit.edu/6.824/2014/papers/plan9.pdf (the 'Plan 9 from Bell Labs' overview paper) plus web research — primary sources preferred (the 9fans/plan9 man pages, 9p2000 spec, 9front documentation). Public-domain or appropriately-licensed images may be downloaded into the book's assets and used, but must be attributed in the figure caption.

images.prompt: An International-style graphic: flat geometric shapes on a white field, black and grays with one Swiss-red accent, strict alignment and generous whitespace. Reductive and rational — a diagrammatic image, no shadows, no gradients, no ornament. Subject: a small cluster of thin-stroke boxes representing files and directories, connected by straight orthogonal lines into a single tree, with one box picked out in Swiss red to suggest a mount point grafted into the hierarchy. No text labels baked in. Target size ~960×1280px, 3:4 portrait; compose for a book cover — the subject sits centred in the upper two-thirds with safe margins, leaving quiet space near the bottom for a title to be overlaid.
